# Offshore North
**Week ending:** August 18, 2026
> **A Toronto Star profile this week placed Scott Shawyer's attempt to become the first Canadian to finish the Vendée Globe inside a lineage that includes both a historic Route du Rhum win and a skipper lost at sea.**

## What This Show Is
Every four years a small number of people sail alone, without stopping and without assistance, around the world. It is the hardest thing in sailing, the kind of race that gets called the Everest of the seas, and no Canadian has ever finished it. Scott Shawyer and Canada Ocean Racing are trying to change that at the Vendée Globe starting 12 November 2028. This show follows that attempt week by week and uses it as a door into the whole sport.

Canadians have history here. A Canadian won the very first Route du Rhum in 1978 by 98 seconds after 23 days at sea. This series is the next chapter of that story.

This sport is reported almost entirely in French, so the stories reach English speakers late and stripped of meaning. This show closes that gap weekly.

The weekly shape is The Canadian Boat for consequence, not recap; The Fleet for the week in offshore racing with the why-it-matters layer; Plain Sailing for one concept explained properly; and The Countdown for days to the start and where qualification stands.

Sources are named and linked every week. There is no hype, no play-by-play that is stale by Monday, and nothing stated that the sources do not support. Uncertainty is flagged as uncertainty.

The show is for lifelong offshore fans, weekend sailors, and people who have never touched a rope and never will. No sailing knowledge is required and none is assumed. Whatever needs explaining gets explained, one clean sentence at a time.

Offshore North is part of the Nerra Network, an independent, ad-free network of daily shows built by two friends covering technology, science, markets, world news and language learning in several languages, free with no ads and no paywall, at nerranetwork.com.

## The Canadian Boat
As of the team's 17 August 2026 update, the most recent public post is the Toronto Star profile; no new boat position is reported.

The Toronto Star ran a feature on Scott Shawyer that links his Vendée Globe 2028 goal to the loss of Gerry Roufs in the 1996–97 race and to Mike Birch's 1978 Route du Rhum victory. Shawyer's first solo IMOCA race was the 2024 New York Vendée on the 2011 Owen Clarke design now named EMIRA IV. The profile frames the campaign against the reality that no Canadian has completed the Vendée Globe. It notes Shawyer came to the sport from business and engineering after 26 years as president and CEO of JMP Solutions. The piece also references the boat's prior history, including its third-place finish in the 2024–25 Vendée Globe under Sébastien Simon despite a broken foil.

This coverage moves the campaign from niche sailing press into mainstream Canadian media, which raises the visibility of the qualification path that requires at least one Grade 2 solo finish on the race boat within twice the winner's time plus a top-37 ranking in the IMOCA Globe Series. Source: [canadaoceanracing.com](https://www.canadaoceanracing.com/article-the-everest-of-the-seas-took-one-canadians-life-and-broke-anothers-dream-hes-going-anyway/)

### The Fleet
Philippe Hartz, after 17 years in the French navy, is preparing an IMOCA campaign for the 2028 Vendée Globe. The profile notes his long service and the personal decision to pursue the solo non-stop round-the-world race. Hartz served in the Marine nationale before turning to the IMOCA class. The interview highlights how military experience translates into the demands of solo ocean racing. No specific boat name or current sponsor is listed in the report.

This adds another experienced solo sailor to the growing list of 2028 entrants and shows how military and offshore backgrounds continue to feed the class. Source: [voilesetvoiliers.ouest-france.fr](https://voilesetvoiliers.ouest-france.fr/ENTRETIEN-Apres-17-ans-de-service-dans-la-Marine-nationale-Philippe-Hartz-poursuit-son-reve-de-Vendee-Globe)

The IMOCA Géodis, winner of the 1996–97 Vendée Globe with Christophe Auguin, is entered in the 2026 Route du Rhum. The boat will race again under its historic name in the solo transatlantic event that starts 1 November from Saint-Malo. It previously carried the name Géodis during its winning campaign. The entry keeps a proven hull active in the current cycle. No new modifications or crew details are reported for this appearance.

Re-entry of a past winner keeps older hulls in the public eye and illustrates how proven designs remain competitive even as newer foiling boats enter the fleet. Source: [voilesetvoiliers.ouest-france.fr](https://voilesetvoiliers.ouest-france.fr/Vainqueur-du-Vendee-Globe-en-1997-avec-Christophe-Auguin-lImoca-Geodis-sera-au-depart-de-la-Route-du-Rhum-2026)

A Scuttlebutt column examined whether faster IMOCA 60s, now routinely sailed from below deck, still meet COLREG Rule 5 requirements for a proper lookout by sight. The piece notes that the class's speed increase has reduced time on deck while the rule itself has not changed. It references the International Maritime Organization convention and the specific wording that every vessel shall maintain a proper lookout by sight. The column questions how the shift to indoor sailing stations interacts with collision-avoidance obligations that apply to all vessels.

The discussion directly affects safety standards and race rules that every solo offshore campaign, including Shawyer's, must satisfy. Source: [sailingscuttlebutt.com](https://www.sailingscuttlebutt.com/2026/08/17/when-does-enthusiasm-become-chaos/)

## Plain Sailing
The Canadian lineage in offshore racing runs through four distinct chapters that together explain why Shawyer's attempt carries weight beyond one person's goal. Mike Birch, sailing the 12-metre trimaran Olympus Photo, won the first Route du Rhum in 1978 by 98 seconds after 23 days at sea when he passed a much larger monohull in sight of the Guadeloupe finish. Gerry Roufs of Montreal lay second in the 1996–97 Vendée Globe when his last message described 15-metre seas and winds above 80 knots; he was never heard from again and wreckage reached Chile months later. Derek Hatfield campaigned Spirit of Canada through the round-the-world races of the 2000s but did not finish a Vendée. Shawyer is the fourth chapter: no Canadian has yet completed the Vendée Globe, and his target is to be the first.

Each chapter shows a different face of the same reality. Birch proved a Canadian could win at the highest level of offshore racing. Roufs showed the sea still decides outcomes no matter the preparation. Hatfield kept a national flag in the fleet for another decade. Shawyer's campaign now tests whether the next step—finishing the non-stop solo lap of the planet—is possible for a Canadian on a current-generation foiling IMOCA.

The through-line is not nationality for its own sake. It is the concrete demonstration that the sport's hardest event has remained just out of reach for sailors from one country across fifty years, and that one active campaign is now aimed squarely at closing that gap. The Route du Rhum victory in 1978 established that Canadians could compete at the front of the fleet in the most demanding conditions. The loss of Roufs in 1997 underscored the permanent risk that accompanies any attempt. Hatfield's sustained presence through the 2000s kept the possibility alive even without a finish. Shawyer's effort on EMIRA IV, a boat that has already completed a full Vendée Globe under previous ownership, now carries the accumulated history into the qualification phase that begins with the 2026 Route du Rhum.

## The Countdown
817 days remain until the Vendée Globe start on 12 November 2028. The campaign's next concrete milestone is the Route du Rhum, which starts 1 November 2026 from Saint-Malo and will be Shawyer's first solo transatlantic race on a foiling IMOCA.
